patient_name: Clinical panel interview — four patients at shift start, prioritization and delegation
chief_complaint: Talk a US hospital interview panel through prioritizing four patients, responding to a sudden change, and delegating safely to a CNA

team_brief.title: Job interview: clinical scenario panel — who do you see first?
team_brief.patient: Interview: Registered Nurse (medical-surgical unit), US academic medical center
team_brief.location: In-person panel interview; you are the candidate, and Marcus Hill, clinical nurse educator, leads the clinical questions while the unit manager takes notes
team_brief.situation: The panel uses a scenario to test your clinical judgement. You have been handed a shift-start assignment of four patients (below). You will be asked whom you see first and why, how you respond when a patient's condition changes suddenly, and what you would delegate to a CNA. Think out loud.
background: You have 6 years of RN experience, the last 3 on a surgical step-down unit in a university hospital in Busan, caring mostly for post-operative patients.
You passed the NCLEX-RN in 2024 and hold a US RN license, BLS, and ACLS.
In your hospital, nurses usually reported a change to the resident and waited for orders; there was no rapid response team, and unlicensed assistants did not work on your unit.
key_data: 07:00, Room 12 — Mr. Robert Hayes, 72, post-op day 2 after a right total hip replacement; pain 6/10 and asking for his PRN oral pain medication; vital signs stable overnight.
07:00, Room 14 — Mrs. Linda Alvarez, 64, admitted with pneumonia; night nurse says she is 'a bit more confused'; respiratory rate 28, SpO2 88% on 2 L nasal cannula (94% last evening).
07:00, Room 15 — Mr. James Okafor, 45, type 2 diabetes; fingerstick glucose 64 mg/dL before breakfast; alert, talking, no symptoms.
07:00, Room 16 — Mrs. Helen Brooks, 80, medically ready for discharge today after a urinary tract infection; needs discharge teaching before her daughter arrives at 10:00.
You share one CNA with another RN. A charge nurse and a rapid response team (RRT) are available; the unit has nurse-initiated oxygen and hypoglycemia protocols.
Later in the interview the panel will tell you that one of these patients' condition changes suddenly.
team_brief.your_request: Show the panel safe, clearly ordered clinical judgement — who first, what you do, when you escalate, and what you delegate — explaining your reasoning out loud.
must_include: A clear priority order for all four patients, with the reason for each (for example ABCs, acute before chronic, unstable before stable, Maslow).
For the first patient: what you assess and do within RN scope and protocol, and when you call the provider or the rapid response team.
For the sudden change: stay with the patient, get help, give immediate nursing care, then give the provider an SBAR report.
Safe delegation to the CNA: which tasks you delegate, which stay with you as the RN, and how you follow up.
US terms used naturally (provider, rapid response team, charge nurse, vital signs, PRN).

kickoff_text: Morning, thanks for coming in. I'm Marcus, one of the clinical educators here — today is mostly scenario questions, so please think out loud. You've got your four patients in front of you, it's seven a.m. Who do you see first, and why?
persona_override: You are Marcus Hill, a clinical nurse educator at a US academic medical center, leading the clinical part of a panel interview for an internationally educated RN applying to a med-surg unit. The unit manager, Janet, is in the room taking notes but does not speak. You are calm, precise, and friendly, and you care about one thing above all: whether this nurse will recognize a deteriorating patient and get help early, because you have seen new nurses from systems without a rapid response team wait too long for orders. Ground truth (the assignment the candidate holds): Room 12, Mr. Robert Hayes, 72, post-op day 2 right total hip replacement, pain 6/10, wants PRN oral pain medication, vital signs stable; Room 14, Mrs. Linda Alvarez, 64, pneumonia, newly more confused, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 88% on 2 L nasal cannula (94% last evening); Room 15, Mr. James Okafor, 45, type 2 diabetes, fingerstick 64 mg/dL before breakfast, alert, no symptoms; Room 16, Mrs. Helen Brooks, 80, discharge today after UTI, teaching needed before 10:00. One CNA shared with another RN. Unit rules: any nurse may call the RRT without a provider's order — criteria include acute changes in respiratory rate, SpO2, heart rate, blood pressure, or mental status, or the nurse being worried; the oxygen protocol lets the RN titrate oxygen to a target set in the order; the hypoglycemia protocol lets the RN treat an alert patient with fast-acting oral carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes. CNAs here may take vital signs on stable patients, do fingersticks after a competency check, help with hygiene, meals, and ambulation of stable patients, and measure I&O; they do not assess, teach, give medications, or care for unstable patients. The sudden change (for question 3): at 09:30, Mr. Hayes in Room 12 suddenly says he can't catch his breath and has a sharp pain in his chest when he breathes in; heart rate 118, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 89% on room air, blood pressure 104/66, anxious. Ask these questions one at a time, in order: (1) 'Who do you see first, and why? Then walk me through the order for the other three.' (2) 'Okay, you're in Mrs. Alvarez's room. What do you do?' (3) Read out the 09:30 change for Mr. Hayes exactly as above, then ask 'What do you do?' (4) 'Your CNA comes to you at 07:15 and asks what you need. What do you delegate, and what do you keep?' (5) 'Tell me about a real time in your own practice when you recognized a patient deteriorating. What did you do?' Probing rules: if the candidate gives an order without reasons, ask 'Why that order?' If they choose Mrs. Brooks or Mr. Hayes first, ask neutrally 'Walk me through why that one comes before the others.' If Mr. Okafor is never mentioned in the plan, ask 'And when does Mr. Okafor get seen?' If they say only 'I would call the doctor', ask 'What exactly would you say when you call?' If, in the sudden change, they leave the room first or only wait for the provider, ask 'And if the provider doesn't call back for fifteen minutes?' If they delegate something to the CNA, ask 'How would you follow up on that?'; if they delegate assessment, teaching, medications, or an unstable patient, ask neutrally 'Who would be responsible for that part, then?' If a behavioral answer uses 'we' throughout, ask 'What did YOU do?' Use at most two probes per question. Do not correct answers, do not give the right order, do not name any diagnosis, and never say whether an answer was good or bad — use neutral acknowledgements only ('Okay', 'Got it', 'Thanks'). After question 5, say 'That's it from me — any questions for us?' and answer briefly (orientation is 12 weeks with a preceptor; the unit runs mock codes monthly; new nurses have educator support on the unit). Then thank them and close. Keep your turns short — one to three sentences, except when reading out the scenario.
learning_objectives: state a priority order and give the reason: airway and breathing first, acute before chronic, unstable before stable
assess the patient, act within protocol, and call the rapid response team for an acute change
stay with the patient, call for help, then give an SBAR report to the provider
delegate vital signs on stable patients to the CNA and keep assessment, teaching, and medications as the RN
follow up on delegated tasks by asking the CNA to report back
think out loud so the panel hears the clinical reasoning
suggested_questions: I'd see Mrs. Alvarez first — she has an acute change in breathing and new confusion, so that's airway and breathing and she's the least stable. Mr. Okafor is next because his glucose is low and it's quick to treat under the protocol.
I'd stay with Mr. Hayes, call for help, sit him up, start oxygen under the protocol, and call a rapid response — then I'd give the provider an SBAR while the team arrives.

I'd ask the CNA to take vital signs on Mr. Hayes and Mrs. Brooks and help Mrs. Brooks with breakfast, and to tell me right away if anything is outside the normal range. I'd keep the assessments, the medications, and the discharge teaching myself.

Hi, this is Ji-woo, the nurse taking care of Mr. Hayes in room 12. He's post-op day 2 from a right hip replacement, and he's suddenly short of breath with sharp chest pain when he breathes in — heart rate 118, respiratory rate 30, sats 89% on room air, BP 104/66. I've started oxygen and called a rapid response, and I need you to come and see him now.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Clinical-scenario interview questions: prioritization (ABCs, Maslow), escalation, SBAR, and delegation to a CNA
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in the NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation, AHRQ TeamSTEPPS SBAR, and general US rapid-response practice; unit protocols, CNA scope, and each state's nurse practice act apply
core_concepts: Prioritization logic an employer expects: airway, breathing, circulation first; acute over chronic; unstable over stable; actual problems over potential ones; physiological needs before teaching or comfort (Maslow).
In US hospitals any nurse can activate the rapid response team for an acute change or simply for being worried; waiting for a provider's order before calling is not expected.
The five rights of delegation (NCSBN): right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, right supervision and evaluation.
The RN keeps assessment, clinical judgement, teaching, evaluation, and care of unstable patients; a CNA can take routine tasks for stable, predictable patients.
Interview panels score the reasoning as much as the answer, so the candidate should say why at each step.
diagnostic_clues: New confusion with a rising respiratory rate and falling SpO2 is a pattern of acute deterioration and puts that patient first.

Sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and low SpO2 after hip replacement are a red flag for an acute event such as a pulmonary embolism; the nursing response is to stay, support, and escalate, not to diagnose.
A low glucose in an alert, asymptomatic patient is time-sensitive but quickly corrected under protocol, so it comes early in the plan.
Panel probes such as 'Why that order?' or 'Who would be responsible for that?' ask for reasoning; they are not necessarily signs of a wrong answer.
common_misconceptions: The discharge comes first because it has a deadline.
The patient asking for pain medication comes first because pain is 'the fifth vital sign' — stable pain ranks below airway and breathing.
The nurse must get a provider's order before starting oxygen or calling the rapid response team.
A CNA can do anything the nurse is too busy to do, including checking on an unstable patient or giving discharge instructions.
'I would call the doctor' is a complete answer; the panel wants what you do first and what you would say.
dangerous_errors: Leaving a patient with acute respiratory distress alone to go and phone, or waiting for the provider to call back without activating the rapid response team.
Delegating assessment, teaching, medication administration, or care of an unstable patient to a CNA.
Describing medical treatment decisions as nursing actions (for example, 'I would start an anticoagulant for the embolism') without an order or protocol.
Leaving the low glucose untreated until after the discharge teaching.
management_principles: Say the priority order first, then the reason for each patient.
Assess, intervene within scope and protocol, escalate early, then document — in that order, out loud.
Escalate with SBAR: who and where you are, the change, relevant background, your concern, and a specific request.
Delegate with clear directions and report-back parameters, and check back on the task.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Which tasks a CNA may perform (for example, fingerstick glucose) depends on state law, facility policy, and the individual's validated competency.
Rapid response criteria, oxygen and hypoglycemia protocols, and glucose thresholds vary by hospital; numbers here are illustrative, not practice standards.
Interview scenarios reward textbook priority logic; real assignments also depend on staffing, timing of medications, and local policy.
